subject: READING
prompt: According to the passage, for whom was the Mercator projection devised?
passage: A map looks like the most honest of documents. It has no adjectives; it makes no speeches. It merely shows where things are. And yet every map is an argument disguised as a description. Because a sphere cannot be flattened without distortion, the cartographer must decide what to sacrifice. The familiar Mercator projection, devised in 1569 for sailors, preserves compass directions at the cost of size: it swells the lands near the poles until Greenland appears as large as Africa, a continent in fact some fourteen times greater in area. Generations of schoolchildren have absorbed this inflated north without ever being told that it was a navigator's convenience rather than a fact of nature. The choices do not end with geometry. Someone decides which towns deserve a dot and which may vanish, where the center of the page falls, and whether a disputed border is drawn as a firm line or a tentative dash. Such decisions are rarely sinister. They are simply unavoidable, since a map that included everything would be as large and as useless as the territory itself. The mistake lies not in making choices but in forgetting that they were made. To read a map well is to ask not only 'Where is it?' but also 'Who drew this, and for what purpose?'
choices: schoolchildren
governments
sailors
African mapmakers
explanation: The passage says the projection was 'devised in 1569 for sailors' and calls it 'a navigator's convenience.'

subject: READING
prompt: What did Semmelweis order his staff to do?
passage: In 1847, a Hungarian physician named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed a grim pattern in the Vienna hospital where he worked. In the maternity ward staffed by doctors and medical students, roughly one new mother in ten died of childbed fever; in the neighboring ward run by midwives, the rate was less than half as high. The doctors, he realized, often came to deliveries straight from performing autopsies. Suspecting that they carried some deadly material on their hands, he ordered his staff to wash in a chlorine solution before examining patients. Deaths in his ward plummeted within months. One might expect that such a result would have been celebrated. Instead, it was resented. Semmelweis could not explain why handwashing worked, for the germ theory of disease lay two decades in the future, and his proposal carried an insult that his colleagues could not forgive: that gentlemen physicians were themselves the agents of death. He made matters worse by denouncing his critics as murderers. Dismissed from his post, he died in an asylum in 1865, his reform largely abandoned. Vindication came only later, when the work of Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister supplied the theory that his evidence had lacked. His story endures as a warning that being right is not the same as being persuasive.
choices: wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients
stop performing autopsies altogether
move all patients into the ward run by midwives
wear gloves during every delivery
correctAnswer: wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients
explanation: The passage says 'he ordered his staff to wash in a chlorine solution before examining patients.'

subject: READING
prompt: What did Mr. Okafor find in the bottom drawer of his desk?
passage: Mr. Okafor had taught chemistry at Linden High for thirty-one years, and on the last afternoon of the last of them he found that he had nothing to pack. The posters belonged to the school. The beakers belonged to the school. Even the periodic table above the board, whose faded corner he had taped and retaped, would stay for his successor, a brisk young woman who had already measured the windows for blinds. He opened the bottom drawer of his desk out of thoroughness rather than hope, and there, beneath a drift of expired hall passes, lay a single index card. 'Dear Mr. O,' it read, in purple ink. 'You said I asked good questions. Nobody ever said that before. I'm going to be a nurse. Dana R., 4th period.' There was no date. He tried to summon a face and could not; there had been, by his rough arithmetic, some four thousand students, and several Danas. He stood for a while with the card in his hand. Outside, the buses were pulling away, and the building was settling into its summer silence. Then he slid the card into his shirt pocket, switched off the lights, and left the drawer open behind him, empty, for whoever came next.
choices: a faded periodic table with a taped corner
an index card from a former student
a retirement gift
a photograph of his first chemistry class
correctAnswer: an index card from a former student
explanation: Beneath the expired hall passes 'lay a single index card' signed 'Dana R., 4th period.'

subject: READING
prompt: According to the author, what would a right-to-repair law require?
passage: When a tractor breaks down in the middle of harvest, a farmer cannot wait two weeks for an authorized technician. Yet many manufacturers now design their machines so that no one else can fix them. Software locks reject replacement parts that the company has not approved; repair manuals and diagnostic tools are withheld from owners and independent shops alike. The same practices govern our phones, our cars, and our kitchen appliances. Manufacturers defend these restrictions in the language of safety and security, warning that amateur repairs could cause injuries or expose devices to hackers. The concern is not absurd, but it proves too much. We allow people to change their own brake pads and rewire their own lamps, tasks far more hazardous than swapping a cracked screen. The more plausible motive is financial: a company that monopolizes repair can charge what it likes, and a device that cannot be affordably fixed must be replaced. The costs fall on consumers, who pay more, and on the environment, which absorbs millions of tons of discarded electronics every year. A right-to-repair law would not force anyone to open a toolbox. It would simply require manufacturers to sell parts and share manuals on fair terms. If you cannot fix what you have bought, in what sense do you own it?
choices: consumers to repair their own devices instead of using a technician
companies to repair all devices for free
a ban on software in farm machinery
manufacturers to sell parts and share manuals on fair terms
correctAnswer: manufacturers to sell parts and share manuals on fair terms
explanation: The author says the law 'would not force anyone to open a toolbox. It would simply require manufacturers to sell parts and share manuals on fair terms.'

subject: READING
prompt: Which of the following statements contain flawed reasoning (a logical fallacy)? Select all that apply.
choices: My opponent's plan for the park must be bad; after all, he was once fired from a job.
Three independent studies found the medicine effective, which supports approving it.
Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be the best one.
The bridge passed a full inspection last month, so it is reasonable to keep it open.
If we let students chew gum in class, soon they will ignore every rule in the school.
correctAnswers: My opponent's plan for the park must be bad; after all, he was once fired from a job.
Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be the best one.
If we let students chew gum in class, soon they will ignore every rule in the school.
explanation: The first attacks the person instead of the plan (ad hominem), the third treats popularity as proof (bandwagon), and the fifth claims without support that one small step will lead to an extreme result (slippery slope). The other two draw reasonable conclusions from relevant evidence.
